title: Three perfect days in Los Angeles: Halloween and the Day of the Dead
dek: Halloween lands on a Saturday and Día de los Muertos fills Sunday, so LA gets a long weekend of costumes, candlelit altars and, with rain likely, some very good museums.

hero.caption: Griffith Observatory on the slope of Mount Hollywood, above Los Feliz and the basin

intro:
Los Angeles does two holidays back to back this weekend, and it does both with real conviction. Halloween falls on a Saturday, which means West Hollywood closes Santa Monica Boulevard for its free street Carnaval and half the city is in costume by dinner. Sunday is November 1, the first day of Día de los Muertos, and the altars are already up: ofrendas fill Gloria Molina Grand Park downtown, and Olvera Street is in the middle of its nine-night observance, with a procession and music each evening.

The other story is the weather. After a warm stretch, forecasters are flagging a wetter Halloween weekend, with the National Weather Service putting the regional chance of rain above 90 percent from Friday through Monday. So this plan leans indoors without apology. LACMA's new David Geffen Galleries, Peter Zumthor's long concrete bridge over Wilshire Boulevard, opened in April and arranges the collection by the world's oceans rather than by century. Across the street the Academy Museum has just opened **The Horror Show**, six galleries of film monsters, which is about as well timed as an exhibition gets.

Friday stays on the Miracle Mile and in Koreatown, Saturday climbs from Los Feliz to the Observatory before a Musso & Frank martini and the Carnaval, and Sunday walks downtown from Grand Central Market to the altars. Pack a real umbrella, and remember the clocks go back an hour early Sunday morning: you get an extra hour of sleep on the one night you'll want it.

days.title: Friday: the Miracle Mile and Koreatown
days.intro: Two great museums face each other across Wilshire Boulevard; plan for rain, then end the night over a grill.

stops.name: République
stops.text: Start under the high wooden ceilings of Walter Manzke's bakery and restaurant on La Brea, where breakfast runs from 8 a.m. Time Out points regulars to the Belgian waffle, the cheesy lobster omelette and the short rib kimchi fried rice, and the pastry case is the reason people queue. The pastries sell out, so earlier is better, and on a wet morning the big room is a good place to wait out a shower. Breakfast service ends at 2 p.m.

stops.name: LACMA and the David Geffen Galleries
stops.text: LACMA opens at 11 a.m. on Fridays and stays open until 8 p.m. The headline is the David Geffen Galleries, opened April 19 and designed by Peter Zumthor: one elevated, step-free floor of about 900 feet spanning Wilshire, with 26 galleries of the permanent collection arranged around the world's bodies of water instead of by date or region. It is a long, absorbing walk under cover. Adult tickets run about $28 to $30; buy ahead online and give it two unhurried hours.
stops.wiki: Los Angeles County Museum of Art

stops.name: The Original Farmers Market
stops.text: A short ride up Fairfax to Third Street, the stalls under the green-and-white roofs have fed Angelenos since the 1930s, and they make the easiest lunch in town for a group that can't agree. Wander the aisles first, then choose: Magee's Kitchen, Singapore Banana Leaf and Seoul Sausage Company are all here, among dozens more. Most of the seating is under cover. The market is open until 9 p.m. on weekdays, so there's no rush.

stops.name: Academy Museum of Motion Pictures
stops.text: Back on Wilshire, the Academy Museum (open until 6 p.m., closed Tuesdays) has the most seasonal show in the city. **The Horror Show**, which opened September 26 on Level 4, moves from a sound installation and a recreated hallway into six galleries (Gothic, Psychological, Science, Slasher, Religion, Ghosts) that draw on *Dracula*, *The Exorcist*, *Halloween*, *Get Out* and more. It is free with museum admission. The museum advises parental guidance; some of it is meant to unsettle.

stops.name: Park's BBQ
stops.text: Koreatown is ten minutes east, and Park's is one of its benchmark grills: Time Out ranks it second in the city. Order the wagyu boneless short rib, the house galbi and the seasoned pork belly, and add the spicy black cod or a kimchi pancake while the grill heats. Book online; it is open until 10 p.m. If you are six or fewer and want something louder, Time Out suggests its sibling KTeam BBQ across Vermont.

stops.name: The Prince
stops.text: Finish in red leather. The Prince is a dim, Art Deco-styled room that has played itself in *Chinatown*, *Mad Men* and *New Girl*, and now runs on Korean bar food and cocktails. A chef writing for Tasting Table last December recommended the unbreaded fried chicken, the chapchae and the spicy fried rice cakes. Even after barbecue, a half chicken for the table is the right call. It is a friendly place to dry off before bed.

days.title: Saturday: Los Feliz, the Observatory and Halloween on Route 66
days.intro: A slow Eastside morning, the city's favorite building, and a costume party the size of a boulevard.

stops.name: Little Dom's
stops.text: The corner Italian on Hillhurst serves breakfast as well as it does dinner, and on a gray Halloween morning the warm room and the ricotta and blueberry pancakes are exactly right. Time Out also likes the meatball sandwich if you'd rather go savory. Reserve on Resy for weekend mornings. Afterward, the DASH Observatory bus stops on Hillhurst, so you don't need to drive or park up the hill.

stops.name: Griffith Observatory
stops.text: Open from 10 a.m. on weekends and free to enter, the Observatory is a good rainy-day plan as much as a sunny one: the exhibit halls and the Samuel Oschin Planetarium (paid shows) are all indoors, and if the clouds break, the terraces look over the whole basin to the Hollywood Sign. The DASH Observatory/Los Feliz bus runs every 20 to 25 minutes from Vermont/Sunset station and Hillhurst; bring exact change, 50 cents, or 35 cents with TAP.

stops.name: Yuca's
stops.text: Back down the hill, this tiny hut on Hillhurst has been the neighborhood's lunch counter for decades. Time Out's Los Feliz list sends people for the double cheeseburger (about $9), and the tacos are the reason the place is famous. There's little seating, so on a wet day take your order to go and eat under an awning or back at the car. The Los Feliz stand closes at 6 p.m.

stops.name: Skylight Books
stops.text: Walk over to Vermont Avenue for an hour in one of the city's best independent bookstores, which turns 30 this fall and is opening a second store in Eagle Rock. Skylight is known for its literary fiction, art books and graphic novels, and the Arts Annex next door covers film, music and photography. Pick up something by a Los Angeles writer for the plane; Vermont's cafés and shops make an easy rainy-afternoon stroll.

stops.name: Musso & Frank Grill
stops.text: Hollywood's oldest restaurant opens at 5 p.m. on Saturdays, and a Halloween dinner in its booths feels like dressing up in its own way. Order a martini, the onion soup, and the filet mignon or the shrimp with sauce poulette, then key lime pie. The dress code is business casual: neat, not formal. Book on OpenTable well ahead for Halloween night, and go early so you're out by eight for the street party.

stops.name: West Hollywood Halloween Carnaval
stops.text: From 6 to 11 p.m., Santa Monica Boulevard between Doheny Drive and La Cienega becomes one long free costume party, with a stage and DJ near San Vicente. There is no parade route; the street is the show, and the costumes are the best in the city. Don't drive: the free WeHo Halloween Ride runs along Santa Monica Boulevard from La Brea to Kings Road until 3 a.m. If it pours, the crowds thin, but keep a poncho, not an umbrella, in the crush.

days.title: Sunday: downtown for Día de los Muertos
days.intro: Breakfast in a 1917 market, contemporary art, then the altars of Grand Park and Olvera Street.

stops.name: Grand Central Market
stops.text: Enjoy the extra hour, then head to Broadway, where the market opens at 8 a.m. and has fed downtown since 1917. Get coffee at G&B, an egg sandwich at Eggslut, or tacos at Tacos Tumbras a Tomas, one of the long-standing stalls. Mains run about $8 to $16. Seats fill quickly on weekends, so arrive early. The Bradbury Building is across the street, and Angels Flight is just outside the Hill Street doors.

stops.name: The Broad
stops.text: Up the hill on Grand Avenue, general admission to Eli and Edythe Broad's collection of postwar and contemporary art is always free, and on Sundays the museum is open 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Book a free timed ticket online; walk-up waits can run half an hour on a weekend. The Infinity Mirror Room on the first floor needs its own free reservation, made in advance, so reserve both at once.

stops.name: Walt Disney Concert Hall to Olvera Street
stops.text: Next door, circle Frank Gehry's steel-clad concert hall, then walk down through Grand Park, where the ofrendas of Downtown Día de los Muertos stand along the terraces (open daily 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. through November 2). Continue across the 101 to El Pueblo and Olvera Street, the oldest part of the city. In rain, wet steel and marigolds photograph better than you'd expect, and the walk is about 20 minutes.

stops.name: Cielito Lindo
stops.text: The stand at the north end of Olvera Street has been rolling beef taquitos under avocado sauce since the 1930s, and they remain the thing to order. The Infatuation's pick is the No. 2 combo: two taquitos, cheesy refried beans and a beef tamal. Eat standing, then walk the street, where community altars are up for Olvera Street's nine-night Día de los Muertos and the festival runs from 10 a.m.

stops.name: Noche de los Muertos at Grand Park
stops.text: Walk back to Grand Park for the closing celebration of its Downtown Día de los Muertos, from 3 to 7 p.m.: DJs, live music, traditional masked performers and other cultural activities among the altars. It is free and all-ages; the park invites an RSVP but no ticket is needed. If you'd rather catch the procession, Olvera Street's La Danza de la Muerte starts at 6 p.m. Note that sunset is an hour earlier tonight.

stops.name: Bavel
stops.text: End in the Arts District at Ori Menashe and Genevieve Gergis's Middle Eastern restaurant on Mateo Street. Order the duck hummus with fresh pita, the lamb neck shawarma and the ossobuco tagine, and share everything. It's a warm, loud room for a wet night. Book through the restaurant's site well ahead. If you have tickets for the 6 p.m. Lakers game, book a late table instead.

stay.name: Sunset Tower Hotel
stay.text: A 1929 Art Deco tower on the Sunset Strip with a spa and the Tower Bar, a short ride from the Carnaval on Saturday night and from Hollywood and the Miracle Mile. The best choice if you want the party on your doorstep and a quiet room above it.

stay.name: Hollywood Roosevelt
stay.text: The historic hotel on Hollywood Boulevard, with a pool painted by David Hockney and the Cinegrill Theater, is a few blocks from Musso & Frank and on the way to Los Feliz. Hollywood/Highland station is close for the Halloween shuttle and the B Line downtown.

stay.name: Freehand Downtown LA
stay.text: A 226-room downtown hotel with a rooftop pool and a well-known cocktail bar, a walk from Grand Central Market, The Broad and Grand Park, which makes Sunday's Día de los Muertos plan easy. Pershing Square and 7th Street/Metro Center stations are nearby for the rest of the weekend.

events.name: West Hollywood Halloween Carnaval
events.where: Santa Monica Blvd, Doheny Dr to La Cienega Blvd, West Hollywood
events.text: The city's big free costume street party, with a stage and DJ near San Vicente. The free WeHo Halloween Ride shuttle runs along Santa Monica Boulevard until 3 a.m.

events.name: Downtown Día de los Muertos and Noche de los Muertos
events.when: Ofrendas daily 8 a.m.–9 p.m. to Nov. 2; closing celebration Sun. 3–7 p.m.
events.where: Gloria Molina Grand Park, 200 N Grand Ave
events.text: A ten-day outdoor exhibition of community altars that ends with an evening of DJs, live music and traditional masked performers. Free; RSVP invited.

events.name: Día de los Muertos on Olvera Street
events.when: Daily to Nov. 2, 10 a.m.–9 p.m.; La Danza de la Muerte 6 p.m.
events.text: A nine-night observance with community altars, nightly music and a procession led by Aztec dancers and costumed 'Living Muertos.' Free.

events.name: Mid City Mercado Día de los Muertos Block Party
events.text: A free neighborhood festival with a community altar, a parade, live music, carnival rides and more than 100 vendors and food trucks, per LA Weekly.

events.name: My Chemical Romance with The Used
events.text: The band's Bowl run ends with Halloween-weekend shows. It's an open-air venue, so bring rain gear and use the Park & Ride or Bowl Shuttle.

events.name: Phoebe Bridgers
events.text: Three nights at the Clippers' arena, near LAX, through Sunday.

events.name: Lakers vs. Toronto Raptors
events.text: A Sunday home game a short walk from the Día de los Muertos events downtown; expect busier streets and trains around the arena.

events.name: The Who's Tommy
events.text: The touring production of the rock opera plays the Pantages through mid-November; an indoor option for a rainy evening in Hollywood.

know: Clocks go back: daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. Sunday, November 1, so set phones and watches back an hour. Sunset comes an hour earlier on Sunday evening.

Rain is likely: the National Weather Service puts the regional chance of rain above 90 percent from Friday through Monday. LA roads get slick and slow in the first rain of the season, so leave extra time and bring a proper umbrella and shoes.

From LAX, the FlyAway bus runs nonstop to Union Station for $12.75 (about 45 minutes; card or app only). Rideshare and taxis leave from the LAX-it lot by Terminal 1; the flat taxi fare downtown is $54.50 before surcharge. Metro riders take the free shuttle to the LAX/Metro Transit Center for the C or K Line.
Metro fares are $1.75 with free transfers for two hours, and tapping a TAP card, phone or contactless bank card caps your spending at $5 a day and $18 a week.

Halloween night: Santa Monica Boulevard closes in West Hollywood for the Carnaval (6 to 11 p.m.). Use the free WeHo Halloween Ride, which runs from La Brea to Kings Road until 3 a.m.; some vehicles connect to Hollywood/Highland station until midnight.
Tipping: about 18 to 20 percent at sit-down restaurants and a dollar or two per drink at bars; tips aren't usually included on the bill.
Sunday downtown is busy: Grand Park's closing celebration, Olvera Street's procession and the 6 p.m. Lakers game all fall on the same evening, so ride Metro rather than drive.
